final_text:
Short answer: The strongest correlates of PFOA (LBXPFOA) in NHANES are other PFAS measured in serum. Non-PFAS environmental biomarkers (metals, phthalate/phenol metabolites, PAHs, pesticides, etc.) show little to no correlation with PFOA.

What you’ll typically see (across NHANES 1999–2018, allowing for panel changes and detection limits):
- PFOS (LBXPFOS): strongest correlate with PFOA (moderate-to-strong Spearman correlations; commonly the top hit)
- PFHxS (LBXPFHS): moderate correlation
- PFNA (LBXPFNA): moderate correlation
- Longer-chain PFCAs: PFDA (LBXPFDE), PFUnDA (LBXPFUN), PFDoDA (LBXPFDO): low-to-moderate correlations
- PFAS precursors (where measured, earlier cycles): MeFOSAA and EtFOSAA show moderate correlations with PFOA
- PFBS (LBXPFBS): typically weak correlation (shorter half-life)

Everything else:
- Urinary phenols (e.g., BPA, parabens), phthalate metabolites, PAHs, pesticide metabolites: generally near-zero correlations with serum PFOA
- Metals (blood or urine): typically very weak to negligible correlations
- This pattern holds in both crude and survey-weighted, log-transformed, below-LOD–handled analyses

Why: PFOA and other PFAS share sources, toxicokinetics (long serum half-lives), and matrix (serum), so they co-vary within people. Most other NHANES environmental biomarkers are measured in urine with short half-lives and different sources, so they don’t track with serum PFOA.

If you want exact top-ranked correlates for a specific NHANES cycle range and age group, I can run a reproducible, survey-weighted correlation analysis and list the top 10 with coefficients.
